A verb that is not one of the limited auxiliary verbs; this is Cambridge's label for the remainder of the verb inventory.
A lexeme that has more than one inflectional form and therefore has a paradigm.
The complete set of inflectional forms associated with a variable lexeme.
A member of the primary part of a verb's inflectional paradigm; the section's lexical-verb table identifies preterite and present-tense forms, while auxiliaries also have negative primary forms.
One of the plain form, gerund-participle, or past participle forms in the lexical-verb paradigm; modal auxiliaries lack this set.
An additional primary inflectional form available to auxiliaries but not to lexical verbs.
A modal auxiliary whose paradigm lacks all secondary forms; some modal auxiliaries also lack a preterite form.

term: invariant present form of modal auxiliaries
gloss: The single present-tense form of a modal auxiliary, used with subjects of every person and number rather than taking a third-person-singular -s form.
The additional person-and-number distinctions displayed by be in its primary forms, compared with other verbs.
A complement directly related to the verb; NPs are its prototypical form in this section.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A complement related to the verb indirectly through a preposition; PPs are its prototypical form in this section.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: An NP inside a PP complement that is connected to the verb indirectly by the preposition.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: The subject in a canonical clause, structurally outside the VP that realises the predicate.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A non-subject complement contained within the VP in a canonical clause.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A verb that has both an intransitive use without an object and a transitive use with an object.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: The entity of which a predicative complement expresses a property; it can function as subject or object of the governing verb.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: The relation of a predicative complement to its predicand, described as subject-oriented or object-oriented.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: An intransitive clause with a predicative complement in addition to its subject and predicator.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A transitive clause containing an object and a further predicative complement.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: The term used here for the complex-intransitive construction with be as predicator and a predicative complement.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: In this chapter, the number of syntactic complements a verb combines with in a clause.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A term for counting semantic arguments rather than syntactic complements; the source notes monadic and dyadic labels in this sense.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: In the terminology distinguished in the footnote, the number and kind of complements a verb takes, contrasted with valency used only for number.

sources.section: §1.1 Types of complement and canonical clause structures

gloss: A lexical category whose members characteristically head NPs, prototypically inflect for number and case, and do not take objects.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: A phrase prototypically headed by a noun and capable, in an appropriate case form, of serving as a clause complement such as subject, object, or predicative complement.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: The typical four-form pattern created by crossing singular/plural number with plain/genitive case.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: Dependents that occur exclusively or almost exclusively with nouns as head, including certain determinatives, pre-head AdjPs, and relative clauses.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

term: functions of NPs beyond clause complements
gloss: The additional PP-complement, subject-determiner, adjunct, modifier, supplement, and vocative functions available to NPs.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: The semantically empty there used as a clause subject, which is treated as an NP by virtue of occurring in a clausal complement position.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: A determinerless NP denoting a role, such as president, that can function as a predicative complement.

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

gloss: The single higher-level syntactic unit headed by an adjective; the phrase may contain modifiers and, where licensed, complements.
The single higher-level syntactic unit headed by an adverb; its possible internal expansions are broadly a subset of those available to AdjPs.
An adjective phrase can function as a clause complement while the adjective supplies the main semantic predicate and be carries tense and subject agreement.
Adjectives almost always denote states, while verbs are commonly used for dynamic situations, although many verbs also denote states.
A rare adjective that takes an NP complement directly; the section names worth and like as examples.
A head word of a PP, classed here without requiring an NP complement or even any complement.
Selection by individual preposition heads among NP, PP, AdvP, clausal, and predicative AdjP complements.
A use of a preposition that expresses grammatical relations or assigned roles rather than an independently identifiable spatial or other meaning.
A use where the preposition contributes a recognisable independent meaning, as distinct from a grammaticised use.
A preposition that heads a PP without a complement; the same lexeme may optionally take a complement, or never take one.
An exceptional PP head that can follow its own complement, as with notwithstanding.
The relative position of a phrase head and its complement; the Cambridge preposition category is not defined by order alone.
A typological term that can cover both prepositions and postpositions without imposing a linear position on the category.
Traditional category of words introducing subordinate clauses; most of its members are classified as prepositions here, apart from the specified subordinators.
A restricted overlap whereby condition or reason phrases can qualify a situation, proposition or speech act.
Discourse prominence or primary stress on an element, distinct from the scopal focus of adverbs such as only.
Whether a constituent can be informationally focused in an interrogative, negation contrast or cleft.
A dependent that affects the truth conditions of the proposition, as a temporal modifier can.
An evaluative dependent not altering whether the described situation occurred.
The capacity of an adjunct class to be targeted by an interrogative expression such as when or why.
The semantic scope of one adjunct relative to another or to negation.
The capacity of a goal or extent to make a clause describe a bounded event.
A situation presented with a terminal boundary, such as an accomplishment with a goal.
An activity presented without a terminal endpoint.
The surface category forming an adjunct, including AdvP, PP, NP, or finite, non-finite and verbless clauses.

term: front, central and end adjunct positions
gloss: The three coarse linear positions of adjuncts, with multiple adjuncts possible in front or end.
A dependent concerning a speaker's communicative act rather than merely the event described.
An adjunct qualifying the status or likelihood of a proposition.
An adjunct conveying a speaker evaluation of a situation, typically non-restrictive.
Positive or negative syntactic status of a clause, diagnosed by its distribution rather than simply by the presence of a negative word.
A test of a clause's positive or negative status using a permitted continuation, confirmation tag, or prenuclear inversion.
A prosodically detached supplementary continuation whose negative form presupposes a negative host clause.
An interrogative tag that seeks confirmation and bears the opposite polarity from the host clause.
A reduced follow-up clause whose connective reflects the preceding clause's syntactic polarity, such as neither/nor versus so.
A negative-marked constituent before the nucleus whose position triggers obligatory subject–auxiliary inversion.
A five-valued formal system categorising clauses as declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative, or imperative.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

term: characteristic use of a clause type
gloss: The typical illocutionary use linked to a syntactic clause type without requiring that use in every instance.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: The characteristic use of an exclamative clause, distinguished from exclamatory delivery of other clause types.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A type of illocutionary force encompassing requests, instructions, commands and similar attempts to influence behaviour.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A particular clause instance belongs to one major clause type, even when the same abstract string admits more than one analysis.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A string whose punctuation, context or intonation allows different analyses as clause types, resolved in an individual instance.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A coordinated sentence in which individual clauses have distinct grammatical clause types.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A clause lacking a verb that can nevertheless bear a clause-type classification, such as an open interrogative or exclamative.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: A repetition or clarification request built on an earlier utterance, superimposed on rather than replacing the utterance's clause type.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: The application of declarative, closed/open interrogative, or exclamative categories to subordinate clauses.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

gloss: The grammatical status usually marked by dependent function or by distinct subordinate form, not equivalent in every instance to being a dependent.
The status of a head clause within a containing construction, even when a different clause also appears in the sentence.
Internal syntactic cues to subordination, including a subordinator, a relative gap, or open-interrogative phrase placement and subject–predicator order.
A content clause licensed as a complement yet internally identical in form to a main declarative clause.
A subordinate-marked clause in an elliptical answer or rare independent exclamatory construction with no governing predicate.
A wh-relative clause functioning as a supplement rather than an integrated dependent, despite its subordinate syntax.
A dependent clause that preserves main interrogative inversion in a restricted construction, with the complete distribution deferred to §5.3.1.
A subordinate content clause with a subjunctive plain-form verb classified as finite rather than infinitival.
A general class including ordinary relative clauses and fused relatives with phrase status.
A construction in the relative family whose constituent is a clause, as distinct from a fused relative NP.
